text: Grassy stunt (locally ជំងឺតឿសមុំ) is a viral/virus-like rice disease transmitted by brown planthopper. Symptoms typically appear about 10-12 days after a plant is infected: the plant produces an unusually high number of tillers, giving it a bushy, grass-like appearance, with leaves that are short, narrow, and pale yellow-green, often carrying small brown or rust-colored speckling. Infected plants remain stunted and generally survive, but fail to develop normally through to maturity, and largely fail to head or set grain, so the practical impact is a plant that lives but produces little or no usable panicle. Risk rises with the size of the local brown planthopper population, and with cropping practices - such as staggered planting dates across a landscape - that keep planthoppers continuously supplied with young rice to feed and breed on. Control follows the same logic as other planthopper-vectored diseases: use resistant or tolerant varieties where available; avoid staggering planting dates in ways that give planthoppers a continuous host supply; keep field edges and surrounding weeds clear of alternate hosts; use balanced fertilizer and avoid excess nitrogen, which favors planthopper buildup; remove and destroy infected plants found in the field; and directly monitor and control the brown planthopper vector population using standard integrated planthopper management. This is a confirmed new addition to the disease knowledge base, distinct from ragged stunt below even though both share the same brown planthopper vector and were described in the same source.
